blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Point estimation uses a single sample statistic as the best guess for an unknown population parameter (recall §1.3): the sample mean x̄ for the population mean μ, the sample proportion p̂ for the population proportion p.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Calculate the statistic from your sample and offer it as your estimate. It is direct and easy to report. A single number, however, says nothing about how far from the truth it might be.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Today’s 30 children at the under-five clinic have a mean weight of 11.81 kg. The point estimate of the mean weight of all children who attend the clinic is 11.81 kg. Nothing in that one number tells you whether the true mean could be 11.5 kg or 13 kg.

points.html: A point estimate is one number computed from the sample. It carries no statement of its precision. Confidence intervals (§7.2) add that.
Not every way of turning a sample into a number is equally trustworthy. §7.1.1 gives the criteria.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: An estimator is the rule (formula) that turns a sample into an estimate. A good estimator is judged on three properties. It is unbiased if its average over all possible samples equals the parameter. It is more efficient than a rival if its sampling variance is smaller. It is consistent if it converges on the parameter as n grows.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Think of the estimator as a marksman firing once per sample. Unbiased means the shots centre on the target. Efficient means they cluster tightly. Consistent means that, as the sample grows, the shots close in on the target.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Recall Sample Variance and Bessel’s Correction (§3.6.2). For today’s 30 weights, dividing the sum of squared deviations by n − 1 gives s² = 3.07 kg²; dividing by n gives 3.07 × 29/30 = 2.97 kg². Averaged over all possible samples, the divide-by-n version falls short of σ² by the factor (n − 1)/n, because the expected sum of squares is (n − 1)σ² (derived in §3.6.2). The n − 1 divisor removes that shortfall: it is Bessel’s correction, applied to make s² unbiased.

points.html: Unbiasedness. E(estimator) = parameter. x̄ is unbiased for μ (recall §6.5) and s² is unbiased for σ².

Efficiency. For normally distributed data both the sample mean and the sample median are unbiased for μ, but the mean has the smaller sampling variance (the median’s is about 1.57 = π/2 times larger in large samples, because their asymptotic relative efficiency is 0.637 = 2/π; proof beyond this book; Shao, n.d.), so the mean is the more efficient estimator.

Consistency. The divide-by-n variance is biased, but its bias, σ²/n, shrinks to zero as n grows, and so does its sampling variance, so it is consistent. A small-sample bias that vanishes with n can be acceptable.

Two meanings of “bias”. Estimator bias, as here, is a property of a formula and often shrinks as n grows. Design bias (selection or measurement bias, recall §6.4) is a flaw in how the data were collected, and no increase in n removes it. A survey of 5,000 households that misses every migrant household is precise and still wrong.

questions.prompt: Explain why Bessel’s correction (dividing by n − 1) is an application of the unbiasedness property.
questions.answer: An estimator is unbiased if its average over all possible samples equals the parameter. Dividing the sum of squared deviations by n gives a variance whose average is only (n − 1)/n × σ², because deviations are measured from x̄, which sits closer to the data than μ does. Dividing by n − 1 instead scales the average up to exactly σ². The correction exists to make s² unbiased.

questions.prompt: For today’s 30 weights, s² = 3.07 kg². What is the divide-by-n variance, and in which direction is it biased?
questions.answer: Divide-by-n variance = 3.07 × 29/30 = 2.97 kg². It is biased downwards: on average it underestimates σ² by the factor 29/30. The bias shrinks as n grows, so the estimator is consistent.

questions.prompt: A point estimate alone is called incomplete. What is missing from it?
questions.answer: Any statement of precision: how far the estimate might plausibly be from the parameter. A confidence interval supplies it.
